title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to generate a fake news article containing an interview between two real people, a finance presenter and a central bank governor, that never occurred. The fabricated article promoted an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform. This represents deployment of generative AI for impersonation and fraud rather than its stated purpose.

The failure was one of access and intent rather than technical capability. The system that generated the content did so without verification that the interview happened, and without human review before publication to an audience. Catching this would have required either limiting who could use the system to generate content about real people, or requiring verification of factual claims before the output reached consumers.

It is not established whether this represents a failure of a single AI tool or a broader ecosystem of scam infrastructure. The reports document that scammers are using AI as one element in elaborate schemes involving fake articles, reviews, and advertisements together, but do not specify which systems generated which components or how they were deployed.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured an interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock that never actually occurred. The fabricated piece described an increasingly heated exchange about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform that Australian authorities warn against. This scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment schemes that use deepfake content and impersonations of celebrities and politicians to deceive consumers.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals that scams using artificial intelligence are becoming more common and convincing. Last year, the regulator removed 19,400 scams overall, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Commonly impersonated figures include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart. Rather than using isolated fake images, scammers now create elaborate webs of deception involving fake news articles, reviews, and advertisements. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers before investing and warns that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy.
